title: Across the Sahara
hook: Muslim traders cross the desert with salt, gold and books

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egypt and the Nile, a land whose faith changed without a single dramatic day. Your line was: slowly, over centuries. What in your own life has changed that way, too slowly to see? Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

A town built of salt. The walls of the houses are blocks of salt, the roofs are camel skins, and the mosque is made of salt as well. Nothing grows there. The people live on dates and grain carried in from far away. The traveler Ibn Battuta stopped at this place, Taghaza, in the middle of the Sahara, and wrote it down with some amazement. He was heading south with a caravan, across sand that punishes a careless traveler, toward the lands along the Niger River. Salt was going south. Gold was coming north. And riding with the camels, quieter than either, came something else. Today: across the Sahara.
screen: `A TOWN BUILT OF SALT.` → `A MOSQUE OF SALT BLOCKS.` → `A CARAVAN HEADING SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Trade was never a stranger to Islam. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ grew up among the merchants of Mecca, and the Qur'an speaks of the caravans of his tribe, Quraysh, setting out in winter and in summer. Commentators connect one verse to pilgrims who wondered whether they could buy and sell on the road to Hajj. In Pickthall's translation: "It is no sin for you that ye seek the bounty of your Lord (by trading)." So a merchant and a believer could be the same person, praying at the side of a camel. Islam crossed the Sahara along these trade roads, with merchants and teachers. A caravan was a moving village. It traveled together, stopped together at the times of prayer, and lived or died by trust. Ibn Battuta describes how his caravan paid one man to ride ahead alone to the next town, so its people could carry water out to meet the travelers. If that rider got lost, everyone was in danger. Salt from the desert went south. Gold from West Africa went north, to the cities of the Mediterranean. And alongside both traveled scholars, copies of the Qur'an, books of law, grammar and prayer. A merchant who settled in a town south of the desert needed a mosque, a teacher for his children, a judge for his contracts. So the towns at the desert's edge became places of learning as well as markets. Salt, gold and books. The salt was eaten. The gold was spent. The books stayed, and were copied, and were taught.
screen: `THE QUR'AN AND THE CARAVAN.` · `A MOVING VILLAGE THAT RUNS ON TRUST.` · `SALT SOUTH, GOLD NORTH.` · `BOOKS STAY, AND ARE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `SALT, GOLD AND BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The practice: share a book. Settle, and breathe. This time, start with a person rather than a book. Let someone come to mind who has a long road ahead of them: a new job, a hard winter, an exam, a first year away from home. What do they need to carry with them? Then look along your own shelf, in your mind, for the book that fits: a Qur'an, a book of prayers, a novel, a cookbook, a book that got you through something. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply keep them in mind, and think about which book, and why. The bell holds the time.
Across the Sahara. The desert trade roads, where salt went south, gold went north, and Islam traveled with the caravans. Today's word.
Your line: salt, gold and books. Today, lend or give one book to someone, and tell them where it came from. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims in West Africa often tell the story of their faith arriving with traders and teachers who crossed the Sahara, and old trading towns at the desert's edge are still remembered as places of learning.

fork.setup: you're in a caravan deep in the Sahara. the next town is still far off and the water is running low. what does the caravan do?
options: push the camels as fast as they can go.
pay one rider to go ahead so the town can bring water out.
turn back to the last well.
fork.reveal: Ibn Battuta describes exactly this: one man rode ahead alone, and the town's people carried water out to meet the caravan. everyone's life rested on his skill.
